assessment.nobel_worthiness: Optical lattice clocks, via the magic-wavelength trapping idea, turned thousands of atoms into a quantum-limited oscillator and pushed fractional uncertainty into the 1e-18 range. This is a measurement-technique breakthrough of the kind that has opened new science (relativistic geodesy, tests of fundamental constants, dark-matter searches, redefinition of the second) and it rests on decades of careful experimental work in laser stabilization and spectroscopy.
assessment.attribution: Katori proposed the magic-wavelength lattice concept and made the first demonstrations. Ye built the lattice clock into the record-setting instrument and tied it to frequency-comb and ultra-stable-laser technology. The two-person configuration looks natural and defensible; other contributors (e.g. Lemonde, Takamoto, Ludlow, Hinkley) exist but the core credit is fairly clear.
assessment.maturity: Independent confirmation across many labs (JILA, RIKEN/Tokyo, SYRTE, PTB, NIST) is thorough, and the instrument is mature. The timing is good; the older ion-trap clock and comb prizes (Hall/Hänsch, Wineland) were recognised earlier, and lattice clocks are now the leading frontier.
uncertainties: The relationship to earlier Nobel recognition of frequency combs and ion-trap clocks could make the committee ask whether this is an incremental step.
The allocation between Katori and Ye, and the role of the Hall/Ye comb and cavity-stabilization work, could be debated; I am not certain of details.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Ultracold atoms in optical lattices realized the Hubbard model in a clean, tunable experiment: the superfluid to Mott insulator transition, quantum gas microscopy and fermionic Hubbard physics. It created a new measurement platform for many-body physics and has clearly opened a field with wide influence on condensed-matter and quantum-information research.
assessment.attribution: Bloch, Greiner and Esslinger carried the key experimental demonstrations and developed the microscopes and fermionic systems; Zoller and Jaksch proposed the theory scheme. Selecting the three experimentalists is defensible, though omitting the theory proposal of Jaksch/Zoller would be criticised. Greiner and Bloch share the Mott transition work, with Hänsch also a key figure not on the list.
assessment.maturity: Results are reproduced by many groups worldwide and the platform is mature. Analog quantum simulation is still moving toward answering open questions in physics not accessible otherwise, so some may argue the major scientific payoff is still ahead.
uncertainties: Whether the committee views the scientific impact as primarily methodological rather than discovery-driven.
Credit division between experimental and theory-proposal contributions; I am relying on memory of the literature.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Atom interferometry has become a precision instrument for gravimetry, gradiometry, measurement of the gravitational constant and the fine-structure constant, and tests of the equivalence principle. The 'measurement limits what we know' argument is strongly applicable, and the field has spawned practical devices for geophysics and navigation.
assessment.attribution: Pritchard demonstrated early atom-beam interferometry with nanostructure gratings; Bordé gave the key theory and the Ramsey-Bordé interferometer; Kasevich and Chu built the laser-pulse light-grating gravimeters. Steven Chu is notably not in the credited names but is a Nobel laureate already; Kasevich-Pritchard-Bordé is a reasonable configuration, though the attribution among Keith, Mlynek, Carnal, Chu and Kasevich is untidy.
assessment.maturity: Many confirmations and commercial/field devices exist, so the field is mature. Applications beyond physics are emerging but the large-scale fundamental physics results (e.g. equivalence principle tests at the 1e-12 level) remain incremental.
uncertainties: Credit is spread across several groups with priority disputes between nanofabricated grating and light-pulse methods.
Chu's earlier Nobel recognition for laser cooling may complicate a fresh prize for the pulse interferometer.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Squeezed light is an experimentally demanding technique that beats the standard quantum limit and is now used in routine operation of gravitational-wave detectors. It is a convincing example of a quantum-optics method leading to real improvement in an instrument and to a broader class of quantum-enhanced measurements.
assessment.attribution: Caves proposed squeezing for interferometers; Kimble and collaborators (with Slusher et al.) made the first experimental squeezing demonstrations; Schnabel and Mavalvala drove the implementation in GEO600 and LIGO. The list has four names, so a prize would need to leave out Mavalvala or Schnabel or Slusher, and the allocation of credit is unclear; Slusher and Walls/Milburn are other key contributors.
assessment.maturity: The technique is confirmed and operating in LIGO, Virgo and GEO600. The impact is large, but part of the credit may be seen as belonging to the 2017 gravitational-wave prize area.
uncertainties: Difficult attribution given at least four plausible laureates plus earlier pioneers not on the list.
Overlap with 2017 LIGO prize and with Kimble's cavity QED work may weaken the case.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: The Cirac-Zoller proposal for trapped-ion quantum computing, together with its experimental realization by Blatt and others and the follow-on quantum simulation proposals, defined a large research programme in quantum information and produced the best-controlled qubits and gates to date. I value that this combines a proposal with persuasive, careful experimental implementation.
assessment.attribution: Cirac and Zoller made the 1995 proposal; Blatt led the early gate and teleportation experiments in Innsbruck. Wineland (laureate 2012) and Monroe/Wineland group experiments are also major contributors, so a Cirac-Zoller-Blatt prize may be questioned for omitting Wineland/Monroe, but the supplied credit is workable.
assessment.maturity: Experimentally mature and confirmed across multiple groups and companies. Timing is plausible, though the Nobel Prize in 2025 and 2022 already addressed quantum-information topics, making the committee cautious about piling up in one area.
uncertainties: Whether Wineland's 2012 prize reduces the case for more trapped-ion recognition.
Proposals versus experiments split in the credit.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Optical readout and coherent control of single NV centres in diamond gave a solid-state qubit and a nanoscale sensor that works at room temperature, with applications to magnetometry, thermometry, biology and quantum networks. It is a measurement-technique breakthrough in line with my interests in coherence in solids.
assessment.attribution: Wrachtrup and Jelezko did the first single-NV optical detection and spin control; Lukin and others developed the quantum-sensing and quantum register schemes (with Hanson, Awschalom, Yacoby, Hollenberg also important). The three-name configuration is plausible but contested because several groups made early contributions.
assessment.maturity: Robust confirmation with an extensive literature and commercial instruments. Sensing applications are growing, though the largest practical impact may still be ahead.
uncertainties: Overlap in credit with Hanson, Awschalom, Yacoby, Hollenberg and Budker.
Lukin appears on several candidates, which complicates a distinct prize allocation.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Cavity optomechanics showed that mechanical oscillators can be cooled to the quantum ground state and controlled with light, enabling quantum-limited displacement sensing and quantum transduction. It extends precision measurement to mesoscopic objects and links to gravitational-wave detectors and hybrid quantum systems.
assessment.attribution: Kippenberg and Aspelmeyer defined radiation-pressure cooling and strong coupling in cavity optomechanics; Cleland reached the ground state in a piezoelectric resonator and showed quantum states of motion in a mechanical object. O'Connell/Cleland and Teufel/Lehnert and Chan/Painter also contributed ground-state cooling, so the three-person configuration is a partial picture.
assessment.maturity: Experimentally well confirmed, but practical applications beyond niche sensing are still emerging and part of the field overlaps the 2025 prize topic on macroscopic quantum devices.
uncertainties: Multiple groups reached the ground state at nearly the same time; priority and credit are contested.
Interpretation of impact beyond sensing is still developing.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Laser excitation of the Th-229 nuclear isomer opens the way to a nuclear clock with enhanced sensitivity to variation of fundamental constants and to new physics. It is an exciting measurement concept and a striking spectroscopic result, which I find attractive as an experimentalist.
assessment.attribution: Peik proposed the nuclear clock idea; Schumm's group developed Th-doped crystals and radiative decay measurements, and Ye's group demonstrated the frequency-comb-based laser excitation and spectroscopy. Other contributors (e.g. Beeks, Tiedau, Thirolf, Shvyd'ko) also played central roles, so credit may be difficult.
assessment.maturity: Very recent (2024-2025); few independent confirmations and no operating nuclear clock yet. The idea is likely premature for a prize, though it may be a strong future candidate.
uncertainties: No accuracy-competitive nuclear clock yet exists.
The precise early credit for the isomer energy measurement is distributed over many groups, and I have not independently verified the details.
